definition: Reasonable enough to be defended against objections or criticism.
example: With only two healthy players left, the coach admitted the team's narrow lead was no longer tenable.
nuance: Tenable describes a position or idea that can withstand challenge, while tenacious describes a person who refuses to let go.
prompt: A student defends her thesis during a school debate tournament.
options: Her thesis remained tenable even after the judges raised three sharp objections.
Her thesis was tenable, so it collapsed the moment anyone questioned it.
The tenable debater clung to the podium and refused to yield her remaining time to the other team.
The links between her points were tenable, held together by the thinnest of threads.
reasons: An argument that survives tough questioning is one that can be defended.
Falling apart under the first challenge is the opposite of being defensible.
This confuses the word with tenacious; it describes claims and positions, not stubborn people.
This confuses the word with tenuous, which means weak or flimsy.

practice.prompt: A scientist rethinks a hypothesis after surprising new data arrives.
options: The tenable new microscope gave the team brighter and sharper images of the cells.
With the new measurements, the old theory is no longer tenable.
The tenable lab assistant repeated the same experiment every night for six straight weeks.
The data contradicted the theory at every turn, which made it more tenable than ever.
reasons: The word is not general praise for equipment; it judges whether a position can be justified.
Evidence that undercuts a theory means it can no longer be reasonably defended.
Persistence belongs to tenacity; the word applies to ideas that hold up, not hardworking people.
Contradicting evidence weakens a claim, so it cannot make the claim easier to defend.
